The European mole (Talpa europaea) exhibits a suite of life-history traits finely tuned to a subterranean existence. At birth, altricial neonates are remarkably small, with a body mass of only 3.25 grams [Wwb = 3.25 grams], a value reflecting the limited energetic reserves a gestating female can allocate while maintaining her own costly burrowing activity. Growth is rapid, however, and by the time nutritional independence is achieved, a weanling has typically attained a wet weight of 52.1 grams [Wwx = 52.1 grams], representing a substantial increase over its initial mass. When studied under the stable thermal conditions of the burrow system, which average 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], the gestation period required for this dramatic development is a relatively brief 28 days [tg = 28 days]. This short intrauterine phase is characteristic of many insectivorous mammals, where the altricial state is an adaptive response to the high metabolic demands placed upon the pregnant female, allowing her to shift a portion of developmental investment to the post-natal period when biparental care, though limited in moles, can still provide some benefit.

The timing of developmental milestones in Talpa europaea follows a predictable chronology under the species' typical thermal regime. The transition from milk to solid food occurs quite early, with weaning completed at just 31 days after birth [tx = 31 days after birth], a duration measured under burrow temperatures of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This relatively short dependence on maternal milk is an adaptation to the high energetic cost of lactation in a thermoregulating, fossorial environment. Following weaning, the juvenile period unfolds, eventually culminating in the attainment of sexual maturity. Under the same mean burrow temperature, females reach puberty approximately 182 days after birth [tp = approximately 182 days after birth] at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This six-month period to reproductive competence allows for the completion of skeletal growth and the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support the demanding reproductive cycle, a necessary condition for a mammal living in an energetically expensive subterranean niche.

Reproductive output in the European mole is a function of both litter size and the frequency of breeding events. A typical female produces a single litter consisting of approximately three pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = approximately three pups per reproductive event]. In favorable years characterized by abundant earthworm prey and mild winters, a female may successfully rear a second litter, yielding an annual frequency of up to two litters per year [F_R_i = up to two litters per year]. This reproductive strategy, observed under the species' normal core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], represents a relatively modest maximum reproductive rate. Such a conservative approach is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival in a stable but energetically demanding habitat, where the costs of reproduction must be carefully balanced against the individual's own future fitness prospects.

Ultimate body size in Talpa europaea is well documented from extensive trapping studies. The maximal adult wet weight, or asymptotic mass, attained by fully grown individuals is approximately 92.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 92.5 grams], a value tightly linked to the biomechanical constraints of tunnel construction and the caloric returns of a diet composed primarily of earthworms and insect larvae. Longevity data for this species are somewhat uncertain, but field and captive records suggest a maximum lifespan of roughly 6 years [am = roughly 6 years] when measured at the typical active body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This lifespan, while not exceptionally long for an insectivore of its size, nonetheless indicates a solid survival capacity in the face of predation, parasitism, and the considerable energetic drain of constant burrowing activity.

Comparative studies across soricomorphs place the life-history strategy of the European mole within a distinctive context. The relatively brief gestation period measured at its typical burrow temperature is consistent with the pattern seen in other members of the family Talpidae, where altricial birth is the norm. Furthermore, the maximum reproductive rate of about three pups per litter and up to two litters per year yields a modest annual output, but this is balanced by the fact that the reproductive lifespan can extend across several years, ensuring multiple opportunities for breeding over an individual's life.
